Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
in the case where the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has two real, distinct eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] with corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.]

Content:
If [MATH: \mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector corresponding to an eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda,] then
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c\,e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}]
gives us a solution that represents a line through the origin parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}.] So, when [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] are real and distinct, we always have two special straight-line solutions:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_1 e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbf{x}(t)=c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2]

Content:
Along the line parallel to the eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}]:

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda<0,] then [MATH: e^{\lambda t}\to 0] as [MATH: t\to\infty,] so trajectories move toward the origin (stable line).
- If [MATH: \lambda>0,] then [MATH: e^{\lambda t}\to\infty] as [MATH: t\to\infty,] so trajectories move away from the origin (unstable line).

Content:
Usually, to sketch the phase portrait, we proceed as follows:

Content:
1. Draw the two eigenvector lines through the origin (one line parallel to the eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and another parallel to the eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2]).
2. Add arrows on each eigenvector line:

- toward the origin if its eigenvalue is negative, or
- away from the origin if its eigenvalue is positive.
3. Add a few curved trajectories that are generally "pulled" toward the stable direction(s) and "pushed" along unstable direction(s).

Item 10 — Tutorial: Classification of Equilibria

Content:
Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Content:
Again, we are considering a linear system
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
in the case where the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has two real, distinct eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] with corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.]

Content:
Recall that if [MATH: \lambda_1, \lambda_2 \neq 0,] the system has a single equilibrium point at the origin [MATH: (0,0).]
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2.]

Content:
First, we describe the straight-line solutions:

Content:
- Along the line parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1,] solutions have the form [MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}\mathbf{v}_1] where [MATH: c_1 \in \mathbb{R}.]

- If [MATH: \lambda_1<0,] it's a stable line (direction).
- If [MATH: \lambda_1>0,] it's an unstable line (direction).
- Along the line parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2,] solutions have the form [MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2] where [MATH: c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.]

- If [MATH: \lambda_2<0,] it's a stable line (direction).
- If [MATH: \lambda_2>0,] it's an unstable line (direction).

Content:
As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

Content:
- Unstable node (source) if [MATH: \lambda_1>0] and [MATH: \lambda_2>0.]
- Stable node (sink) if [MATH: \lambda_1<0] and [MATH: \lambda_2<0.] In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.
- Saddle point if [MATH: \lambda_1\lambda_2<0] (one positive, one negative).
